Even mountains fall to the tide

by Lilliae

Summary

Mydei was submerged up to the chest yet his tail burned. Scalded with the heat of the underwater forges that had moulded and tempered the weapon that didn’t creak in his hands even as he grabbed with all his strength to keep himself grounded because—

Because it was scales molting from flesh. Bones snapping and rending. Muscles and skin stretching and growing to accommodate.

He dunked below the water and silenced his scream, bubbling to the surface as nothing but empty air. His gills worked as the pain seared up through his hips into his torso: stomach spasming with the urge to wretch, lungs scorching like they were taking on blood instead of air, heart quivering as his most vital organs panicked over the sensation of his body being torn apart from the inside out. Smashed and jumbled back together.

It was an ordinary patrol and return to Styxia. Mydei only needed to report the same fact he had been relaying for years: no changes in the coastline of Aedes Elysiae.

Except he returns to find the village consumed by flames and the black tide. If Mydei wants to help then he has to step onto dry land, which means splitting his tail for the very first time.

Notes

The problem with really liking childhood friends Phaidei is that I’m gonna have to keep finding new ways to write the destruction of Aedes Elysiae.

See the end of the work for more notes

chapters.title: Even mountains fall to the tide
chapters.html:
The most alluring of siren songs summoned a time when the sea was a home. Their voices stirred the settled sands of the seabed to uncover what lay beneath the surface: schools of sirens gliding alongside the undercurrents and the fish, scales glinting in as many hues as the iridescent sunlight splintered by the waters, as they indulged in play and song honouring their god and creator who so relished in the revelry thrumming through the depths. 

Something Mydei had heard but never seen. By the time he was plucked from the boundary between Phagousa’s waters and the Sea of Souls as a mere child, much of the ocean had succumbed to the incursion of the black tide. To him, the tides and currents were merely battlegrounds he could never conquer but bled for regardless.

Ones displayed on the stone slab laid out before him. A map of Amphoreus’ waters and coastline etched into the stone table of the sea cove serving as the war room, illuminated by the sunlight spilling through the gaps in the ceiling and then plants that glowed a pale blue hue. 

“The waters off Aedes Elysiae remain stable for now,” he reported. 

Staring down at the map, Helektra’s dark ear fins twitched at the news. She hummed, almost as indifferent as her placid expression if not for the slightest upturn of acknowledgement at the end as she reached for the broken and smoothed shared of a dark sea shell.

All sirens were older than Mydei but only few could boast of their seniority to Helektra, numbers dwindling as the war against the black tide dragged, yet they had all remarked at one point or another on how similar the two of them were. Unreadable expressions. Unwavering dedication. Unmatched battle prowess. 

But it was always with a forlorn crease to their faces, voices ringing with the low tenors of mourning, when they went on to explain how cheerful and carefree she had once been. Her voice had crested with every wave and broken with the sea foam only to begin anew as they carried her song, calling for others to join her in harmony, to every corner. 

“Peace is fleeting. Savour it while it continues to fill your chalice,” her melodious voice ended with the clipped finality of the shell shard upon the stone, ever closer to a familiar coastline. 

When faced with the black tide, stable never meant unchanged. The encroachment was consistent but constant, like the passage of the sun stretching shadows longer and longer to darken what had once been bright. Incremental enough to miss without observation of the minute details—until the moment it surged. 

Four years had passed since Mydei first surfaced along the coasts of the village unmarked on Helektra’s map, languishing in the sun alongside the wheat it farmed. It was an ordinary patrol turned violent by an unforeseen encounter with the black tide. 

There had been no major upheavals since, which meant he should have been redeployed elsewhere. He was the youngest of the sirens and still resembled a child more than the adolescent he was growing into. But there was a reason Phagousa had been so quick to fish a human child from the Sea of Souls and transform them, even when they had long since lost the strength to breathe new life into scales and sea foam. 

Dark tides will taint our crystal currents, so we shall summon the sacred waves, draw the filth into the Grand Chalice, until Strife shines back against the black tide… 

To happen upon a child of Strife in such unusual circumstances was taken by the Ocean Titan as a sign. From what or whom Mydei was never certain and he was in no position to ask the Titan, slumbering beneath the Golden Chalice to preserve their strength until there was nothing left to protect.

From fate? But wasn’t it fate that had abandoned Amphoreus to this protracted end that he had been drawn into?

To combat the black tide. That was the sole reason he was rescued from a lifetime of drowning in the souls of the dead and their sorrows. 

There was always a region of the ocean in greater need of his skills and undying body. It was only due to Helektra’s interference that he was stationed in the waters of Aedes Elysiae, and called upon elsewhere when needed to bolster the ranks against a surge of the black tide.

They never discussed her generosity. When Helektra seemed reluctant to mention it, the most Mydei could do was fulfil his duties. As such, her decision remained beyond reproach from any siren daring enough to question Phagousa’s most skilled and favoured Titankin. The one who bled gold like the Titan themself. 

Mydei could only assume that an eye such as hers, which peered into the darkest depths of something no longer the ocean she once loved and issued orders without blinking, had taken one glance upon his first return and known. There was something out there. Something of immeasurable value to him. 

The gleam of a starved deep sea beast glutting themselves on sunlight for the very first time. It was a look he recognised in other sirens but had never expected to wear himself. 

After all, sirens were territorial by nature. Over the prettiest shells they dug from the shoals, or the most beautiful pearls and scales they shed. Over the sea coves they claimed as home and decorated accordingly. Over the most comfortable soft corals and the cutting weapons forged for their hands alone. Most importantly, over the tides and undercurrents fought for with every breath. 

Even back then, Helektra had seen it: one of the very first signs Phagousa’s blessing had sunken deeper than skin and scales and into the crevices of his mind. Rather than scorn him for it, she had helped him feed the droning note of longing.

Despite how his vocal cords trembled and his tail twitched with the urge to give into the urge and return to a place he called his own, he left the war room for the reef. It would be unwise to make the journey back without resting first, and he may even be scolded if the exhaustion showed itself too blatantly upon his arrival. 

The sea floor off Styxia’s coasts were far from the vibrant home Mydei had once been introduced too. A place where scales glittered, throwing all sorts of colours he had never seen before into the iridescent sunlight and across the variegated coral reef. 

The black tide had yet to arrive but its disruptions were felt even in this final safe haven. It disturbed water temperatures and currents, migration patterns and food chains, tides and the resonance of waters that once sang with life even without the accompaniment of sirens. 

Still far from the black infection splintered by an unnatural orange, the corals were leeched of their colour and the fish less numerous as the life was bled from the ocean. Behind curtains of kelp and shells, many of the siren’s sea coves were empty of their owners and their possessions had long lost their lustre with no one to care for them. 

Only with explicit permission were sirens permitted to touch another’s belongings. Back when more sirens than he could count swam between the coves, Mydei had witnessed the consequences of such a transgression himself, garnering ire, competition, compensation and even punishment depending on the extent of their wrongdoings. 

So each home was the same as its owner had left it. As though they would return to everything they had once held here—a memorial to the deceased that had come to outnumber the living. 

Perhaps if Mydei had never seen the reefs before they were past its prime whilst still able to echo it, he would be able to witness its dying remains without looking away. But this was a place yet to give way to a lifeless grey heralding the black tide’s arrival even as everything wilted under the knowledge that, one day, it would. 

To some, the sea was no longer the home they had spent centuries luxuriating in under Phagousa’s guiding currents. No matter how the sirens levelled weapons and voices at the creatures that emerged from the light-devouring darkness, they could only hope to slow the invasion draining the warmth from the waters and the sirens of their strength.

To others, Styxia’s shoals lived up to its reputation of temptation, intoxication and revelry. In music, in dance, in wine.

Regardless of the reason, land had become preferable to many of them even as they continued to defend their home waters. The ache of shedding their scales and rending their tail into two legs was manageable so long as their brethren were there to sing and soothe them through the pain. 

Supposedly, the pain lessened with every transformation. Something that the other sirens eagerly recounted to him as a means to tease him above water. 

But, from the waters, Mydei could feel the pulse of life imbibing in Phagousa’s blessings for the sake of self-indulgent pleasure. His nose wrinkled at the drunken drag to every melody thumping as the city’s heartbeat, yet drifting wayward compared to the assured currents and tides that pointed to battle and then retreat and battle again. He had little interest in experiencing it for himself. 

All of his fascination and curiosity was reserved for one place. For now, he only had the barest hints of it nestled away in his sea cove at the outer edges of the reef, right where it began to slope into deeper waters. The location was held in low esteem, practically hidden from any companionable eyes as even the sunlight struggled to reach inside and illuminate the small space. It was why the cove had been empty when he joined the reef so much later than Phagousa’s Titankin created long before his birth.

The sirens had clamoured to offer him a better home but he preferred the privacy as he dropped the sea kelp curtain behind him. His body was small and he rarely lingered in the reef for long, so the smaller space relative to the other caves didn’t bother him. It was only in recent years he had gained much to decorate the space with beyond old polite gifts, given by other sirens until they realised he didn’t share the same eye as them to covet the same items. Shiny things. Pretty things. 

The possessions closets to the bed of soft corals were the exact things they would pass over. A small bronze dagger cared for upon every return to prevent the green hue emerging. A stone carved with an image near unidentifiable as the wheat fields that inspired it. A necklace of ordinary shells clumsily tied together with twine. 

Only he would smile at such things as he inspected them for any signs of tampering or erosion while he was away. Nothing to find, he returned to their proper places and laid down to rest in preparation for his long journey. The city and reef thrummed through stone and water, trying to lull him to sleep when he longed for another place entirely. 

Aedes Elysiae was a wheat farming village. Many people fished but their main produce was wheat. The houses were old and wooden but cared for to prevent rot. There was one schoolhouse and one courtyard dedicated to the Titan of Time said to watch over the village. A statue of Oronyx overlooked the town centre. Above a small pond was a swing set with rope that creaked when sat upon but had yet to ever fray or snap. 

Although Mydei had never seen the village for himself, these were among the many things he knew about it. At most, he had dared to observe from a distance, eyes peeking just above the water dyed dark by the night. But the moon’s illumination and his own bright hair and eyes deterred him from acquiescing to the temptation of sneaking closer. 

Instead, he lingered in that inlet and sea cove carved from the cliff faces. It was trickier to manoeuvre through the shallows during low tide but he could always draw the tide higher with a pluck of his lyre strings and voice. Besides, he preferred the company where the sea met the sands. 

After all, it wasn’t Mydei who made a home of that drab sea cove—but Phainon. 

Phainon, who gathered fresh bouquets to decorate the cave and place the spares—there were always spares—in Mydei’s hair despite objections that the salted water would ruin them. 

Phainon, who left a fishing pole and bait in the back corner so he could lounge on the sun-warmed stones beside Mydei, spending half a day fishing them dinner when Mydei could catch enough to feed his entire village in the time it took a cloud to pass over the sun.

Phainon, who always restocked on medical supplies and treated Mydei’s wounds, grim-faced; although, his hands had stopped shaking around the time they grew long and calloused from working the fields. Mydei had once showed him how muscle and blood vessels knitted themselves back together without interference but the sight hadn’t comforted him as Mydei assumed it would. 

Phainon, who gaped when Mydei admitted he had never encountered wheat and brought a stalk of it the next day. Although Mydei had never seen nor felt it—golden, hollow and brittle when matured. Allegedly green, smooth and firm when too young to harvest—he already knew it by scent. It paired well with the salted sea breeze ruffling through Phainon’s hair scented like the fields he farmed and played in. 

Phainon, who brought such warmth to the waters of Aedes Elysiae that no others could compare. Before Mydei first surfaced and happened upon him there, all waters felt so similar they would have been indistinguishable if not for Phagousa’s blessing, guiding him with a depth of innate knowledge that rivalled their oceans. The only exception were the frigid seas around Aidonia but even those roused the same notes as he flicked his tail and thrust his trident. Free, comfortable. 

The ocean was still those things to him. It was Aedes Elysiae that had become more. It was red and gold flowers bobbing in the gentle waves, a wheat stalk and sunlight just as golden tickling his cheeks and nose, and a smile that could illuminate the deep sea but chose to shine on Mydei alone.

It’s waters should never have felt so frigid that Mydei shivered as he crossed into territory that had always greeted him so warmly. His tail pushed against dense waters, thicker than Aidonia’s near frozen sea, and his gills burned as they worked to filter the water into something breathable. 

Scents didn’t carry through water as they did air. All of his senses were attuned beyond that of any ordinary mortal and many sirens—eyes in need of little light, fins detecting the faintest vibrations—but smell required focus when even the strongest of them were subdued by the ocean.

Yet Mydei’s nose twitched with an overwhelming rot. 

His grip tightened around his trident. His body was tempered to act even as his mind denied what was plainly in front of him. Denied what exactly was tainting the currents pushing him away to safety as much as they drew him in to fulfil his duty. 

It wasn’t golden sunlight and wheat fields that greeted him when he broke the waters closer to the pier than he had ever dared to venture. But the scorching glow of the firelight and a glaring orange ravaging through Aedes Elysiae to blacken it beyond even ashen remains. There would be nothing left. 

The black tide.

Acrid smoke choked his lungs, his gills, and he gagged but didn’t dive back into the safety of the water. He had yet to encounter any black tide creatures lurking in the depths nor beginning to surface. They must have already made land.

He was too late. Or had the black tide waited for him to leave before surging forth, knowing there was no one to guard against its claim to the seabed sloping up onto dry land  

He shook his head. The black tide wasn’t a sentient mass: it was an affliction, an infection. Alive, but only just enough to have an instinct to consume everything different from itself. To spread. 

It was a lost cause. Once the black tide spilled into clean waters or split the earth open and embedded itself into all the cracks, there was no purging it. Aedes Elysiae was gone. 

He should turn back. Return to Styxia. Shrug off this failure of his and look elsewhere for the next boundary between life and evernight in need of his protection. If the black tide progressed at this speed, it would likely be Styxia itself. 

But his heart twisted with the snarl of his lips, fangs bared and fins flared, as he gripped his trident. Aggressive. 

Defensive. More than any ocean current or coral reef, there was something here that was Mydei’s. So the course of action was as much a painful inevitability as the tide towed by the moon. 

Mydei was submerged up to the chest, yet his tail burned. Scalded with the heat of the underwater forges that had moulded and tempered the weapon that didn’t creak in his hands even as he grabbed with all his strength to keep himself grounded because—

Because it was scales molting from flesh. Bones snapping and rending. Muscles and skin stretching and growing to accommodate. 

He dunked below the water and silenced his scream, bubbling to the surface as nothing but empty air. His gills worked as the pain seared up through his hips into his torso: stomach spasming with the urge to wretch, lungs scorching like they were taking on blood instead of air, heart quivering as his most vital organs panicked over the sensation of his body being torn apart from the inside out. Smashed and jumbled back together.

It was a fact that he was born with two legs. Phagousa had taken them, blessed them, and stitched them together into a tail in the same moment his blood sprouted scales. But he was still frozen by death in the Sea of Souls when the Ocean Titan and their Titankin had lulled him into a more merciful state, half-dazed and half-asleep. Any memory of that transformation was beyond his grasp. For the better. 

Now, there was no one. He could only grit his teeth, clench his fists, scream where no one could hear, and endure. 

But that was what he was best at. As the child left to drift down the River towards Death only to be rejected, his body and soul were shattered and reforged countless times over into something stronger, sturdier, sterner than steel because he could fracture but never truly break again. 

Whether abandoned to scrape together the remnants of his life from the clutches of the dead in the Sea of Souls, to oblige the god that had rescued him by raising his spear against the black tide in their name, or to fight through the pain of his wounds ripping open and stitching themselves back together again—he could endure it all. He could survive anything. 

So he endured until the sweltering pain numbed his limbs. The faintest tingles remained at the very extremities. Thighs, calves, toes: they were long unused but not forgotten. He kicked with two legs in place of a tail, slowly reaching for the world darkened by smoke and corrosion just beyond the water’s surface. 

He was close enough to the pier that he secured his trident between his teeth and hauled himself up. His arms trembled, fins flared, with the phantom pain of his legs splitting still wracking through him but he dragged himself onto the pier. 

It was hardly a challenge when his deceptively slim body harboured the strength to crush bones. Yet his arms gave out and he flopped onto the rough wood, heaving and coughing to expel the smoke clinging to his lungs. All he got was empty air and speckles of bloodied water where his cheek bled with his own teeth marks. 

Too vulnerable. He needed to move. Staying still was a death sentence. 

But the moment he tried to stand fire lanced through his legs. Like walking on knives, each step split his soles open and pierced through the bone arching his feet. His head bowed and his trident clattered to the ground as his mouth dropped in a scream. No water to muffle it, he grappled at his own throat to strangle the sound before the wounded noise could make him the sole target of stronger predators.

Pearls rolled down his face in place of tears, dripping like the saltwater from his hair and skin and staining the wooden pier in a splattered ring around him. Dark with water but no blood, despite how he felt the life draining through his feet. 

He bent to reclaim his trident and his quivering calves were near collapse, a mound of sand about to be knocked flat by the oncoming waves. If he hit the ground, laid down and let his legs relax without the weight of his body over them, he would never rise again. Not even when a black tide creature loomed over him with an instinct to gut him and bleed him dry.

His muscles begged for relief, for respite, but he clenched his jaw and forced himself upright. One step. Just one to start with. Then another, and another, and another. Until he was walking with all the graceless stammer of a newborn.

Faster. He needed to be faster or he was no better than limping prey, a fish with a ripped fin incapable of catching water. He needed to run. 

The world was blurred by smoke and his own mind dizzier than the time the other sirens had playfully pushed him into whirlpool, sweeping him around and around and around until it finally spat him out, giddy with laughter instead of delirious with the pain. 

He barked a rough laugh, more a pained exhale, as he slumped against a roofed storage area next to the pier. He grabbed at it to keep his balance as he raised himself onto his toes. Every muscle from the waist down twitched, spasming out of control as he forced them to flex when they wanted to slump back into one long limb. 

Did his body recall how to run? He must have done it as some point. He remembered. Distantly. When he was lucky enough to hit the rare shallows of the Sea of Souls and given the briefest reprieve from drowning. There he could stand and sprint away from danger, knowing it would snatch him up and tear him apart and drag him back into the abyss but never when. 

Now he sprinted into danger. Suffocating heat and smoke choking the life and memory from the village. Blood splattered red, black and orange across the worn grounds and old wooden buildings. Tall shadows shaped just wrong as they moved—too long here, too short there, too bulbous and glowing and devouring light.

He cut one down with his trident and moved onto the next sprouting like waves birthed droplets of water when they crashed against the shore. Each fleck of orange was unnatural, almost glowing but not from the firelight flickering off it; so unlike anything that should exist, let alone dare to mimic life. Across his bare feet and calves, it was akin to poison seeping through his skin into his thoughts. 

Why? Why was he still here? Everywhere he looked was carnage. Even Thanatos had abandoned this place. It was beyond the reach of Death as it succumbed to the black tide. The swing of his trident would do nothing to hold it back or deter it. He only added to the destruction laying waste to a small village that would no longer grow wheat. No longer catch fish. No longer glow golden in the sunlight. 

It would never again be a peaceful village living alongside the ocean, playfully splashed by the tides. It had been consumed by the worst of it: scented not with salt and the world beyond but an inescapable decay. 

There was nothing for him here. 

He screamed. Anguished and aggrieved and more animal than human as he lunged at a black tide creature. It wasn’t his trident that pierced its chest but his bare hands as he gouged it open with his claws. He felt for that pulsing orange core and ripped it out. 

Sirens fought with elegance. Every step, sway, swing flowed like the current. They moved to a melody innate to waves and sea foam that birthed them, only to be imbedded in their enemies with a strike of their weapons that sang with the sea’s beauty and destruction.

There was no grace, no poise. None of the finesse of a siren nor a human as he fell back into his old instincts with the despair he had known once by feeling and not name. Back when he only had his hands, his feet, his teeth to fight off enemies strong enough to crush his small body with hardly a thought. A child more acquainted with pain and Death than anything else. The only things he knew because nothing else existed in the Sea of Souls where he was more dead than alive. 

He crushed a black tide creature’s arm with a snap of his jaw. One hand grappled at its face and the other grabbed its upper arm and he pulled. A chattering screech rattled his brain but he clamped his teeth and yanked harder until black blood sprayed across his face. It’s arm tore free from its shoulder and he spat the severed limb to the ground. He lunged again and the rest of the creature joined it in shreds. 

More. He wanted more. Craved it. The only things he craved more was a sunlight that had been snatched away and extinguished in a darkness deeper than the night. To punish these creatures for their insolence in their trespassing and transgression was the next best thing to slake himself on. 

Perhaps his feet were still protesting, beseeching him to retreat while he could. Perhaps it was the earth scorched hot by the flames as he prowled the village’s hollowed out remains. All he cared about was wetting his teeth and feeding an appetite he knew would never be sated. 

But over the howling winds sweeping embers, death and rot to taint his lungs was a voice. One capable of stirring the winds, the waves, and drop a speck of light that cleared the smoky, delirious haze over Mydei’s watery eyes. It sounded like his own. In its anguish. In its rage. In its all-consuming grief. 

But he could never mistake that voice. He knew it too well. 

He staggered past the statue of Oronyx crumbling with their protection and up the hill to the courtyard and swing set. His feet trembled. Whether relief loosening his muscles or a newfound fear of that relief being crushed, he stumbled upwards with the weight of the ocean and black tide clinging on to drag him back down. He had to know. To see it for himself. 

Another scream and the inhuman screech of a black tide creature. A death wail. 

Mydei crested the hill and his breath caught like he was breathing water instead of air. Through the grime of blood and smoke, it was unmistakably white hair beneath the dirty grey, moving with a body still strong enough to swing the dulled edge of a sword that Mydei would know anywhere because he had gifted it himself.

Phainon slashed through a black tide creature and swiped gold from his cheek as he watched it fall. Eyes utterly blank. The face of a corpse forced to keep standing, drifting aimlessly. 

But he blinked and life flickered across his widened eyes. His lips moved, soundless beneath the carnage setting Phainon’s entire world ablaze around them. Mydei saw the move of his lips and knew what that one word was. He had heard it countless times over the years every time Phainon glimpsed him surfacing from the water or languidly reclined, half-submerged and half in the sun, waiting for Phainon to arrive. 

His name. Always. Joyful surprise and a relief that let Phainon’s next breath come easier knowing Mydei was there with him in a small, insignificant village when the rest of the world called for him to be elsewhere and die there. 

Mydei lurched forwards and the sheer relief weakened him from the heart outwards. The sudden quiet in his ears made him realise how loud it had pulsed. Until now, when it calmed at the simple sight of Phainon rushing towards him. 

His legs buckled and Phainon caught him. 

“Mydei,” Phainon breathed heavy, skimming warm across the blood dried tacky to his face. “What are you… your tail—your legs.”

He grunted and tried to reclaim his slumped weight slumped, only for Phainon’s arms to tighten and hold Mydei against him. “Focus on what’s most important.”

Their lives. Phainon was alive but alone. There were no bodies still resembling a human anywhere in the vicinity. Besides them it was safe to assume there were no other survivors. 

Phainon’s brows furrowed over his lowered eyes. “You’re shaking.”

He grabbed Phainon’s hands to break his firm hold, shifting his weight onto his own feet. Given the briefest reprieve of Phainon shouldering his weight, the pain lanced through him anew. He suppressed a wince. There was no time to waste on Phainon’s trivial concerns on his behalf. 

“We need a route out of the village.”

The disapproving set of Phainon’s face was unconvinced but he didn’t sweep Mydei from his quivering feet into his arms. Despite the slow clench of his hand into a fist, he released it with a weighty exhale and hooked an arm around Mydei’s torso, resting it beneath his armpit to bear as much weight as Mydei would give him. He turned their backs on the courtyard. 

His sword cut through the thickets and low branches, leading the way while Mydei limped at his side. The branches and brambles stabbed his soles but the pinpricks of pain were hardly noticeable when his feet were a few steps from being completely numb. 

He was enough of a burden—lower body nothing but dead weight and hands devoid of any weapons after losing his trident—if he mentioned the state of his legs even once he would have to fend off Phainon’s insistence on carrying him. 

Especially as his sword remained brandished but largely unused. The black tide creatures were still clustered around the village and yet to disperse through the outskirts in droves. They encountered two among the trees but Mydei peeled himself away from Phainon’s side and he dispatched them with ease. 

They staggered away from the coastline and through the golden wheat fields. It was almost harvest season, grain scratching his thighs as they trampled through. The long stalks swayed with a wind that should have carried the scent of sea salt and earth tones of wheat. But it was the stench of death choking his lungs with smoke and embers. 

When the time for harvest came, the fields would be left to rot. Assuming the black tide didn’t destroy them first. 

Where the fields were no longer tilled and sowed, a small cabin was nestled between the forest and the wheat. Phainon sent him a questioning look and Mydei, through sweat and gritted teeth, nodded. They were far enough for now. For what remained of the night. 

The black tide moved steady but slow outside of the occasional surges. It cycled between periods of high and low activity, only the when was never certain. That unpredictability was one of its most terrifying attributes. It necessitated constant patrol from a dwindling pool of manpower, and their best wasn’t always enough. 

Mydei was away for less than a week and Aedes Elysiae was gone. 

That etching on a stone slab of a coastline and village without a name would soon be buried under black shards. Helektra would cast her eye elsewhere, and expect Mydei to follow as the spear at the end of her sword. 

The cabin door was unlocked and Phainon awkwardly guided them through the doorway too narrow to walk through side-by-side. Mydei’s attempted to shrug him off but the shove was so weak Phainon didn’t even entertain him. 

The cool press of Phainon’s hand, steadfast around Mydei’s waist, was the last thing he could feel before the exhausted stretch of his legs, flipping with each step between numb and the anguish of flesh being sliced down to the bone. 

The cabin was bare inside. A hearth and some chests but nowhere to sit. Phainon nudged him towards the wall and Mydei shivered at the dig of cold stone into his back. He slid down, slow and steady. Phainon followed him down to catch him if his legs gave out as they should have done the moment he made land. 

It was the sort of thing Phainon did with a smile, even a teasing jab or slight jest, daring Mydei to retaliate as he picked seaweed out of his hair or massaged the feeling back into his arm after he fell asleep in an unfortunate position. 

Yet his head was lowered, gaze and thoughts hidden. Not that Mydei needed to see Phainon’s devastated expression to know it was there, and all the ugly thoughts that came with it. 

Only once Mydei was sat with a harsh exhale did Phainon back away to dig through the chests. After so long of enduring past his limits, there was no relief from being off his quivering feet. 

His body healed all wounds yet this one was so persistent. He could only hope the pain would vanish by the time he woke up. If not… he always was adaptable. They needed to be on the move tomorrow morning. Midday at the very latest. The more distance between them and the back tide the better. 

But they both needed rest first. Phainon’s movements were both sluggish and stiff as he returned. His eyes were open but glazed as he dropped the straw mat from under his arm, hitting the floor in a plume of dusty grit. It was mechanical when he knelt down to unroll the sleeping mat and dump a stack of fabrics into a loose bundle on top, lacking all of Phainon’s usual attentive, if clumsy, care. 

The only consolation was that his slack face and hazy eyes weren’t quite the same as the look Mydei had first found him with. That had been vacant. Dead. The end of an inferno that had burned bright and fast only to scorch itself to embers just as fast. 

Now, Phainon was simply lost. 

In all the time Mydei had known him, Phainon was quick to talk. It was how he expressed joy, always so eager to share it with others, and suppressed his worries in the same breath. But he had hardly spoken since they trekked away from his hometown burning up in ash and smoke like a funeral pyre to everything he had been and known. He could only hope enough of Phainon survived somewhere beneath the wreckage. 

Neither of them were in a talkative mood. Mydei’s body and voice had been all but eviscerated, and his heart continued to waver in his chest, leaving him lightheaded and breathless. Still…

“Sit,” Mydei commanded with as much steady authority as he could muster. 

A lazy blink. Then a glance from Mydei’s face to his legs and back up again. Phainon’s throat worked around a swallow and he rasped out, “There’s a river nearby. To wash off.”

The mention of cleanliness reminded Mydei of the sheer amount of filth clinging to him; the closest the black tide could come to claiming his life. His nose wrinkled and his scales itched at the dried blood and grime. Up until now, all of his battles had been waged in the water, naturally washing away all evidence of strife with the same efficiency his body healed its attempts to mar him. 

“How near?” he asked, doubting his ability to stand, let alone walk anywhere. 

Not close enough to feel with his senses attuned to all of Phagousa’s waters, the mother of the ocean and all rivers. Although, he wouldn’t be surprised if he missed it with the state of his mind and body. 

“Not far. This cabin was built to use in harvest season if anyone lost track of time and couldn’t make it back before dark,” Phainon explained, dull and flat. 

Mydei picked at the straw mat’s fraying edge. “No.”

“I’ll carry you.”

“You—“ His head whipped up, ear fins flared and lips twisted in a snarl, but Phainon’s face made any humiliated vitriol fade.

The day had been far too long for Phainon. The evidence of it stained his skin, bruised and burned and scabbed over in places that would never heal unscarred. His sword was still grasped tight in his hand, hung by his side but twitching with the memory of cutting down creatures, each kill heavy with the possibility that it may have been friends and family twisted beyond recognition.

It was a mercy. It was survival. It was cruel to those who were meant to live long, peaceful lives, and Phainon who would have to carry this new burden on his hunched shoulders. 

Yet his wide eyes and thinned lips were pleading. 

Mydei swallowed. “Fine.”

The vigorous nod of his head was the most energetic Mydei had seen him since he last left for Styxia a lifetime ago. He sheathed his sword and crouched down, arms slipping under Mydei’s knees and behind his back. As though Mydei was no different from the sacks of grain he had spent the harvest season heaving with his family, Phainon hauled him up with ease. 

While one hand cradled a bundle of clothes separated from the blankets left behind on the draw mat, Mydei’s other arm hooked around the back of Phainon’s neck. It was a token gesture, even as Phainon shuffled them through the doorway, as awkward as their initial entry. Mydei had no fears of being unceremoniously dropped. 

Just as Mydei suspected, the river was further than Phainon had made it seem; much too far to limp back and forth from the cabin. Not that it mattered anymore as Phainon kicked off his sandals and stepped into the water, soaking the hem of his trousers, so he could sit Mydei on the bank. 

The meandering river’s shallow depths hardly rivalled the ocean. It was a drop of rain compared to all the waters he had swam in. But his entire body slackened with the relief it brought to his feet. 

Carefully, Phainon slid Mydei’s tunic over his torso, his head, and raised arms. His eyes, bright and keen, gazed across the exposed skin with the same intensity as the moonlight illuminating the lines of Mydei’s body. Unmarked, but Phainon didn’t seem to believe it. 

He folded and set Mydei’s garment aside as though it were precious rather than scrap soon to be burned, purging the corruption too deep to be washed away. Mydei could have lowered himself into the water from there but he remained seated, savouring the coolness seeping into his scales and muscles, while Phainon stripped himself with much less consideration. He was too hurried, rushing to pick Mydei up again and set him chest deep in the river. 

His sigh blended with the froth of the water, washing over him and lulling him to relax like a mother rocked a child to sleep. He watched through heavy eyelids as Phainon leaned over the riverbank, rifling through the pile of new clothes and returning with a rag. 

Although he dunked it, he stared at Mydei both questioningly and expectantly. The huff of laughter through his nose disappeared downstream at the audacity only Phainon could make charming, and he offered his arm. 

It was filthy. The water loosened the dirt and lifted the least stubborn of it all. But the red of his claws, scales and markings were near imperceptible through the black and orange gore that tainted him up to the elbow. The rest of his arm contended with the flecks of aberrant blood amidst the smear of smoke and ash. 

The rough material of the rag was made gentle in Phainon’s hands. While he pressed hard enough to rub the decay away, even using his own nails to dig the gore out from under Mydei’s claws, he was was cautious not to catch his scales or rub Mydei’s skin raw enough to sting. There was only the satisfaction of being clean again, from his webbed fingers to his shoulder. 

Once he was satisfied with the one arm, he dunked the rag again and wrung it clean, clouding the waters dark only for it to be carried away. Each pass of the rag swept off the stubborn grime that had fought to drag Mydei into the pit of a contamination worse than the frigid ruins of death. 

Gradually, Phainon revealed the redness pulsing underneath. His thumb dragged over his clean claws, nail dipping into a chip Mydei had failed to notice. Then the scales across the back of his hand and wrist, finger pad catching on the spaces that didn’t lie quite flat. His touch fluttered over the markings trailing like flames blazing across Mydei’s cool skin. As the vestiges of battle were washed away to reveal the one familiarity that remained, Phainon breathed easier.

He followed the markings up the side of Mydei’s neck but couldn’t go further than the curve of his jaw. His reflection had given him a glimpse of the mess slathered across his face. It was almost enough to make himself look away. He didn’t know how Phainon witnessed the proof of Mydei’s worst nature and came closer anyway, treating him as fragile instead of savage. 

There was less to clean where the tunic had protected Mydei’s torso but Phainon wiped the dips of Mydei’s clavicle, water pooling dark and trickling down to be chased and swiped away.

Scales clustered around his chest, protecting his vital organs, yet they were more sensitive than protective as Phainon dragged the rag over them, eyes flicking up to meet Mydei’s when he shivered at the faint touch. But Mydei didn’t stop the drift of his hand to the gills by his ribs and down his stomach. 

There was so little skin and flesh to his back that any extra attention was unnecessary, yet Phainon knelt behind him and swept his long hair over his shoulder. He started at his nape, which Mydei could accept likely needed more than a quick splash, but he continued beyond where skin met the watery expanse of Mydei’s back. 

It was unsullied. Mydei knew as much. But Phainon followed the curve of Mydei’s shoulder blades and the dip of his spine like there were wounds in need of care when it was the one section of Mydei’s steel body even more inhuman than the rest. 

His hair required the most tending to. It was scraggly, clumped with knots, soot and blood. If he were alone, he would have accepted his losses and cut it off. Instead, he abided by Phainon’s voice in his ear, so soft spoken and yet too loud to ignore as he encouraged Mydei to sink down to his neck and lean against Phainon.

Phainon’s hands carded through the damp tresses. There were more knots than anything but Phainon tenderly worked at it each one until it unravelled and continued to the ends. Then he angled Mydei’s head further back and scooped water into his cupped hands to pour it onto the crown of his head. He massaged at Mydei’s scalp, lifting dirt to rinse away with another cupped handful of water. 

Once it ran clear, he guided Mydei to sit up again and waded around to Mydei’s front. He knelt and propped Mydei’s foot on his leg. He started at Mydei’s thigh but there was little dirt to linger over, dragging the rag over the knob of Mydei’s knee and the crease at the back. Below was where the carnage truly began. 

Despite being submerged for so long, his legs appeared as though he had waded through scum rather than water.

He had. With the searing pain of his muscle and bones restructuring, resetting into a form they had forgotten, the acrid blood as much an affront to nature as himself, the scorched earth and smouldering ashes, the cut of jagged stone and splinters slicing his soles open—those had almost been a reprieve. If his mind had cared enough to think about them beyond the brief acknowledgement that the sensation meant he was still alive enough to wreak more havoc. 

His legs were also the least cooperative part of his body. They twitched at every pass of the scratchy fabric over his calves, his ankles, or his feet. The only place Phainon could effectively clean were his shins and his skin still prickled like the plate of bone wanted to jump out. 

When he rubbed the rag over the outer bone of Mydei’s ankle, thumb circling the inner knob, Mydei’s entire leg flinched back. He was only stopped by Phainon’s hand around his ankle, who peered through his lashes, head bowed, in silent question. Mydei glanced away, ears hot despite the coolness of his hair, but relaxed his foot into Phainon’s hold in answer. 

His hand slowed over the top of Mydei’s foot, toes curling and arch twitching, as he asked lowly, “Does it hurt?”

Myde’s head snapped back around to Phainon’s head and eyes lowered between his hunched shoulders. “No.”

A thumb pushed against his sole and he hissed the beginnings of a harsh breath before biting down the rest. But the kick of his foot—back. Forward. He wasn’t certain—was telling enough. 

Phainon’s head lifted, still sullen but oddly determined when he met Mydei’s eye. “Don’t lie.”

A rough sound rumbled in his chest but he didn’t dare unpin his lip just yet, so he huffed a strained laugh, breathed, and retorted, “Don’t throw baseless accusations.”

“Baseless?” Phainon echoed, voice controlled and neutral as he resumed cleaning the top of Mydei’s foot. 

“Entirely,” Mydei ground out. 

His thumb pushed in again, prodding muscles that were undeniably sore and skin still tender from being burned raw, cut open, and healed again. But that wasn’t the reason Mydei shuddered, stomach flexing and lungs fluttering with a sound Mydei desperately swallowed down. 

Then Phainon’s thumb shifted to the inner curve of his foot while the rest of his fingertips, as a consequence of the rest of his hand moving rather than a thoughtful action, brushed the outer side of Mydei’s foot and he couldn’t stop it in time. 

A laugh bubbled across the river. 

They both stopped. 

Slowly, Phainon raised his head, eyes wide and lips agape. Mydei dug his fingers into the riverbed. The heat had spread from Mydei’s ears to his cheeks and he stubbornly averted his eyes. 

“Mydei.”

“What.”

“Are you—“

“No.”

“But you—“

“No.”

Out the corner of Mydei’s eye, Phainon’s shoulders tensed and Mydei’s ear fins twitched, sensing danger. He wrenched his leg back but Phainon’s grip tightened into a vice around his ankle. It was with purpose when he tossed the rag to free his hand and drag his fingertips in a whisper of a touch down the arch of Mydei’s sole.

A harsh laugh escaped him and his hands jumped to his mouth but the sound was already gone, like air bubbling to the ocean surface. There was no denying it now. Mydei squared his shoulders, ignored the warmth seeping down his neck, and met Phainon’s eye.

“You’re ticklish,” he whispered, thin with disbelief.

“Perhaps.”

Phainon tickled his foot again and Mydei choked on another laugh. The assault didn’t end, Phainon too committed to stealing the laughter from him, high and breathless. 

He had endured worse than this. His body being torn apart one limb at a time. A weapon piercing his flesh to corrode him from the inside out. A tail being split down the middle by his own will. Phainon tickling his foot should have been nothing. 

But he thrashed uselessly against Phainon’s firm grip, growing weaker but more desperate as his torso clenched painfully around every frantic giggle. 

“S-stop,” Mydei stuttered out between cackles stretching his cheeks until they ached as much as his stomach. “S-stop. I am—I am.”

“You are what?” Phainon teased, almost too quiet to be heard when Mydei’s laugh crashed across the river like breaking waves. 

“Ticklish,” Mydei admitted with the last of his breath and kicked his foot out. 

It slammed into Phainon’s chest and sent him sprawling backwards into the water with a splash. Mydei swiped at his wet cheeks that left pearls to be taken by the river. He panted, submerged gills working to help him catch his breath, and Phainon just watched with wide eyes glowing warm in the moonlight reflecting off the river and Mydei’s pale skin. 

His lips twitched and Mydei recognised the upturn of his lips and crease of his eyes but he could hardly believe in when Phainon threw his head back and laughed. Mydei startled at the sound, at the sight of Phainon alight with joy—so familiar and yet…

How had Mydei been so foolish to think it would disappear with the rest of Aedes Elysiae. 

Mydei laughed. Not coerced nor a reflex. But because it was such a precious sound and the part of Mydei that was more siren than human longed to intertwine it with his own into a beautiful melody. 

Eventually the sound faded beneath the river but it wasn’t to be mourned. Mydei could only feel its gain rather than loss. Phainon’s smile mellowed into something exhausted and wistful yet tinged with a gentleness as he gazed at Mydei, right in front of him, with a look that made his weakened heart squeeze. 

He thumbed at a smear of dirt left behind on Mydei’s foot. “Why did you…”

Mydei’s toes curled. “My judgement was impaired.”

It had been a terrible, irrational decision to split his tail and walk on dry land for the first time since he was born. He was vulnerable and in no state, physically nor mentally, for combat. 

In the moment, it hadn’t been a choice. 

The one thing Phagousa feared was the vast solitude of loneliness. They became the mother of all waters and all that lived in them, but that fear was passed onto their Titankin as something deeper: an innate instinct. Territorial by nature, sea sirens coveted things to belong to them, just as they coveted to belong to something. To somewhere or someone. In the vast ocean, each siren was a single note singing out. Every note yearned to be part of a melody. 

It could be a duet or a concerto but Mydei had witnessed what happened when that accompaniment was broken. 

No siren had escaped the war against the black tide unscathed. Each of them had lost someone. The black tide infected their bodies, twisting them into their basest forms, devouring reason and self. Former allies added to the surging wave of enemies to be felled—ruthless and without remorse. The same as their hollowed husks would tear into any siren foolish enough to cling onto past memories.

Mercy. Survival. Burden. When a siren lost the one’s dearest to them it was the same as death. They lost the will to sing, to battle, to live—they simply drifted. 

He had seen but never understood. After all, Mydei was unlike any of the others. They were Phagousa’s Titankin, formed by their hands to populate their waters with life and music, while Mydei was lucky to be plucked from certain, unending death and blessed by those same hands. They never scorned each other but they could never fully understand each other either. 

To the rest of them, Mydei had been the one drifting. The one who swam off on his own to patrol the sea depths while claiming his unique disposition made him suited to individual missions. He rarely joined them in play or song whether on Styxia’s shores or sea coves. He held fast to his duty, to repay the Titan that rescued him no matter their self-interest, but that was all. 

No wonder Helektra and the rest of the sirens had been so agreeable in stationing him near Aedes Elysiae. It was the only time Mydei had settled rather than drift. So when he believed he lost everything, lost Phainon…

He pressed a hand to his heart. Beating strong against his palm as though it hadn’t nearly given in a mere few hours ago. 

“Can you change back?” Phainon asked and Mydei blinked away from thoughts. Phainon resumed cleaning Mydei’s foot, taking extra care to avoid tickling him with the rough rag as he scrubbed the underside of his toes and clarified, “Your tail. Can you go back? These cause you a lot of pain.”

“So long as I have access to Phagousa’s waters,” Mydei explained as Phainon changed to clean his other foot and he stifled a laugh with a bite of his lip before continuing, “But it would be a waste of energy. The waters here belong to the black tide now. The only way for us to reach Styxia will be by land.”

Phainon’s head jerked up. “Us?”

“Why does that surprise you?” Mydei returned with equal confusion.

Beneath the water, Phainon wrung the rag out, dying everything dark for the moment it took to gather his thoughts and courage, “Well…”

“Your thoughts are too loud. Just speak your mind.”

“I’m just a boy from a farming village,” Phainon blurted and immediately looked away, perhaps sighting Mydei’s expression, brewing with a storm rolling in over the horizon, or masking his own embarrassment. “And you, well, you are quite literally a miracle blessing from a Titan. You said Styxia is the city of dreams and intoxication and is full of other sirens and I…”

“So?” Mydei said, keeping the seething bite from his voice but not quite dulling its scathing edge. “Are you doubting my judgement?”

“Wha—no.”

“Good. Because I made my choice.”

A long time ago. So long Mydei couldn’t recall the exact moment it was made, if there even was one. He didn’t realise it was up for debate in Phainon’s mind. 

His fingers caught on the scales over his chest as he dragged upwards in search of the right one. The one, glistening a brilliant red more akin to the heated passion of living than the golden blood that flowed through his veins, that was settled directly over the tip of his heart. He plucked it free with the barest twinge of pain and speck of blood, enough to startle a protest from Phainon that was swiftly silenced by the thrust of Mydei’s hand. 

Moonlight gleamed red in his palm.  “Take it.”

The red eclipsed Phainon’s eyes, breaths shallow. “Mydei, this is…”

He took Phainon’s wrist, holding his palm open so he could place the scale in the centre. “If anyone ever doubts you—“ including Phainon himself, “—this is the evidence. I chose you, Phainon.” 

Tentatively, those fingers curled, clenching tight enough to imprint the pattern into Phainon’s skin. 

Since Mydei was already clean, he took the discarded rag from the river back and motioned for Phainon to exchange places with him. Unlike Mydei, each swipe through the grime of battle exposed its other markings: shallow cuts already scabbed over and deeper ones that had stopped bleeding but still gaped open, bruises beginning to mottle different hues of pain, the corruption of the black tide.

Mydei’s voice failed to sweep it all away so he shed tears for Phainon and silently thanked his golden blood that would accept such a potent blessing from Phagousa as Mydei crushed those pearls against his wound. 

Throughout, Phainon was silent. Thoughtful rather than vacant. But his fingers skimmed against Mydei’s thigh whenever he thought Mydei would fail to notice.

“It’s normal for a siren to suffer when their tail splits,” Mydei soothed whatever needless guilt Phainon may have left. Neither of them were so foolish to pretend the reason Mydei had mounted land was less than obvious. 

“You can endure more than anyone,” Phainon said, anguished at the idea of Mydei’s hardships. “Surely any other siren would be inconsolable. Incapacitated.”

Mydei pinched his chin to tip it back. “Their pain is soothed by the singing of other sirens.” 

Phainon’s attempt to glance back was chattered by Mydei’s hand carding through his hair tightening, keeping him in place as he doused him with water. He was careful as his claws brushed and rinsed out the grey, leaving his hair pristine. As though the day’s tragedy had never occurred. 

But—once they redressed in the clothes Phainon pillaged from the cabin. Too large for Phainon and even larger on Mydei but they would have to suffice for now—Mydei was still too weak to return on foot. Phainon wordlessly picked him up and Mydei didn’t offer an apology or gratitude beyond the rest of his head against Phainon’s chest, listening to the steady beat of his heart in time with his footsteps. 

Once inside, Phainon set Mydei down on the straw mat and retrieved another for himself. Only to unfurl it and push the two together so they laid on their backs beside each other to rest. 

Still, he left a small distance between them. It was ridiculous. They had laid closer together when they lounged on the sun-warmed sands and stones, or when they tussled in the shallow shoals and collapsed into the waters beside or even on top of one another. 

Mydei rolled to face him, pressing into his side. All the permission he needed, Phainon rolled too and draped an arm over Mydei’s waist right where it should have split between flesh and scales but was now smooth skin all the way down. 

“Mydei…” Phainon breathed, eyes half-closed but determined to stay open no matter how sleepily he gazed ahead. 

Mydei leaned to bump their foreheads together. “Sleep, Phainon. You… had a long day. Morning isn’t far off.” 

Phainon hummed but it was an empty placating noise while his hand drifted down to Mydei’s thigh. “Does it still hurt?” 

“Only a little,” Mydei admitted. The same as the ache in his arms after a good battle or spar. “Nothing I can’t handle.”

Yet Phainon shuffled closer still, somehow scrounging space to eliminate. He tucked Mydei’s head beneath his chin, their torsos almost flat against each other. So Mydei felt it when Phainon’s chest rumbled with the beginnings of a hum. Before the noise resonated through the air. 

Singing. Low notes and murmurs that rang through Mydei’s ears and stirred memories like a hand through the sandy seabed. It was waves gleaming in the sunlight that warmed the waters and the salt breeze, golden like the wheat stalk teasing earthy tones beneath his nose. 

A lullaby in Aedes Elysiae. Mydei had heard it once before, billowing with the waves as Phainon waited for Mydei to return to the coasts where he waited so diligently, unaware that he lurked just beneath the surface. After catching Phainon’s voice in a way Mydei had never heard before, he couldn’t reveal himself. Not even to sing in unison when all he desired in that moment was to listen.

So Mydei knew the song well enough to hum along in the depths of his chest. No longer aching. No longer on the verge of breaking and shattering and piercing him from the inside out. 

Their troubles would rise again with the sun. But, for now, his legs settled into their existence and tangled with Phainon’s own as his voice, his scent, his warmth lulled Mydei into dreams of a calm sea beside the wheat fields.
